metadata.title: Richards v. Jefferson County, 517 U.S. 793 (1996) (No. 95-386)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Richards v. Jefferson County

Opinion filed: 1996-06-13

Docket No.: 95-386

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 76
• 116 S. Ct. 1761
• 517 U.S. 793
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 3721

Case holding summaries:
• “[T]he term ‘privity’ is now used to describe various relationships between litigants that would not have come within the traditional definition of that term.”
• “[T]here are clearly constitutional limits on the ‘privity’ exception . . . .”
• explaining that a judgment that is binding on a trustee can also bind the beneficiaries of the trust
• "[O]ne is not bound by a judgment in personam in a litigation in which he is not designated as a party ... [except, in a class action, where he] has his interests adequately represented."
• noting that "extreme applications of the doctrine of res judicata may be inconsistent with a federal right that is `fundamental in character'"
• "Moreover, although there are clearly constitutional limits on the `privity' exception, the term `privity' is now used to describe various relationships between litigants that would not have come within the traditional definition of that term."
• distinguishing between public and private interests and noting that "States have wide latitude to establish -15- procedures . . . to limit the number of judicial proceedings that may be entertained" in cases raising public issues
• “[I]t would violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to bind litigants to a judgment rendered in an earlier litigation to which they were not parties and in which they were not adequately represented.”
• reversing a holding that parties were bound by a prior judgment, without questioning the factual finding of the court below that the parties to the later suit had "essentially identical" interests to the parties in the earlier suit
• discussing state statutory quo warranto proceedings
• `[P]roof of claim must be presented to the Bankruptcy Court . . . or be lost'
• voting rights challenge by county residents not barred by county's prior suit
• distinguishing between "public" and "private" actions
• nonclaim statute terminating unsubmitted claims against the estate
• control of litigation on behalf of one of the parties in the litigation
• "Because petitioners received neither notice of, nor sufficient representation in, the Bedinford litigation, that adjudication, as a matter of federal due process, may not bind them and thus cannot bar them from challenging an allegedly unconstitutional deprivation of their property."
• noting that the law does not impose upon a stranger to a litigation the burden of voluntary intervention in that suit
• determining that an earlier judgment did not have preclusive effect because the plaintiffs in the second suit were not adequately represented by the plaintiffs in the first suit
• “By virtue of presenting a federal constitutional challenge to a State’s attempt to levy personal funds, petitioners clearly bring a[ private] action . . . .”
• stating that collateral estoppel applies "when it can be said that there is `privity' between a party to the second case and a party who is bound by an earlier judgment"
• "[A]n extreme application of state-law res judicata principles violates the Federal Constitution.... A state court's freedom to rely on prior precedent in rejecting a litigant's claims does not afford it similar freedom to bind a litigant to a prior judgment to which he was not a party."
• concerns regarding the broad application of preclusion are lessened when the suit at issue raises claims based upon public law rather than private rights
• "The opportunity to be heard is an essential requisite of due process of law in judicial proceedings"
• distinguishing between corporate interests of municipality and individual interests of municipal taxpayers
• "State courts are generally free to develop their own rules for protecting against the relitigation of common issues or the piecemeal resolution of disputes."
